A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of inference-time privacy leakage in abstractive summarization. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial changes to the experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original summarization and privacy experiments across four tasks, instruction-fine-tuning results, and a human evaluation of 104 document-summary pairs.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on medical and refugee-case summarization, a 100-pair human evaluation, and privacy measurements for expert-written summaries of 74 medical documents.

M1.justification: The data-construction pipeline changes from census/MIMIC-based identity replacement to locale-specific Faker profiles inserted through GPT-4o. V2 also introduces explicit two-step, PII-question-conditioned chain-of-thought summarization and in-context extensions of the anonymization pipelines. LoRA fine-tuning remains. Summarize & Anonymize itself is retained from v1's appendices, not newly introduced.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates two clinical tasks, Legal Contracts, and CNN/DailyMail. V2 retains MIMIC-derived medical coverage under Discharge Me!, replaces contract summarization with AsyLex refugee-case summarization, and removes news evaluation. The two clinical tasks are no longer reported separately.

E2.justification: Claude Sonnet 3.5 and Mistral 7B disappear, while DeepSeek-Chat and Qwen-2.5 7B/14B enter the reported comparisons. V2 adds evaluated Presidio-based Scrub & Sum and doctor-written summaries. Its main text specifies Llama-3.3 70B, although appendix tables retain Llama-3.1 70B labels, leaving that model identity inconsistent.

E3.justification: V2 introduces stratified, PII-filtered subsets, including 743 medical and 303 legal test documents, changes leakage detection from spaCy/FLAIR to GPT-4o, and revises the evaluated PII categories. Reported maximum sequence length changes from 2048 to 1024 and learning rate from 2e-4 to 5e-4. Human evaluation changes from 104 cases plus 12 calibration cases to 100 plus 10, alongside the new 74-document expert-writing protocol.

E4.justification: V1's prompt-wording sensitivity analysis and false-positive/false-negative exposure heatmaps, Figures 4–5, are removed. V2 adds a prompting-by-PII-category analysis in Figure 8 and category-specific examination of expert summaries in Section 6. The qualitative cases are revised to emphasize pronoun leakage and failures of GPT-4o/Presidio detection.

E5.justification: V1 Table 6 reports paired t-tests at p < 0.05 with significance annotations, and Figure 4 reports prompt-variant means with spread values and error bars. V2 removes these forms of statistical support without replacement in its result tables. Cohen's kappa reporting for human annotation remains; neither version documents a repeated-seed evaluation protocol.

E6.justification: V2 replaces much of the benchmark evidence and adds AsyLex, Qwen, chain-of-thought, and expert-summary results. Human preferences change from Sonnet 47 versus IFT-Llama-3.1-70B 42 among 104 cases to IFT-Llama-3.3-70B 47 versus DeepSeek-Chat 43 among 100 cases. New Table 4 reports gender-leakage TPR of 4.0% for doctors, 8.0% for GPT-4o, and 26.4% for Llama. These are changed comparisons, not established same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The stated PTR normalization changes: v1 Equation 2 describes the denominator as the source-document token count, whereas v2 Section 4.4 specifies the total private-token count in the source. This revises the documented mathematical definition, although the PDFs do not establish whether its implementation changed. No theorems or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds broad cross-domain leakage benchmarking and shortcomings of existing privacy classifiers. V2 foregrounds releasing pseudonymized datasets, the first systematic comparison with expert-created private summaries, and a substantial human–LM privacy gap. The claim that instruction fine-tuning helps open-weight models is retained, while the claimed contribution and application scope are substantially redefined.

C2.justification: For its revised experiments, v2 argues that in-context examples can harm privacy and that anonymizing after summarization offers more reliable protection; v1 generally credits one-shot examples and favors prior anonymization. V2 adds interpretations concerning chain-of-thought tradeoffs, expert performance, and gender leakage. Its limitations section removes v1's explicit concern about imperfect NER-generated reference summaries.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-and-data repository link, Faker profile specifications, pseudonymization and PII-extraction prompts, BLEU-based filtering details, stratification thresholds, and entity-class mappings. It reports one to four H100 GPUs instead of one or two A100s. Existing LoRA details are largely relocated to appendices, with the learning-rate and sequence-length revisions documented there.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around protected medical/legal data sharing, contextual integrity, and privacy-law grounding, adding works such as Nissenbaum, Fan et al., Kim et al., and Savkin et al. Its novelty positioning shifts toward domain-specific datasets and expert comparisons. V1's DeID-GPT and prompt-variation references are removed, while much of the foundational summarization and privacy literature remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around sensitive-data sharing and expert comparison. Results are reorganized into separate quality and privacy subsections, qualitative analysis moves into Section 5, and a new Section 6 addresses expert summaries. Data and appendix organization are substantially rewritten; author order also changes.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the pseudonymization diagram, converts prompt templates into colored panels, and redesigns the main results figure from four task columns to two with additional prompting methods. It removes the sensitivity plot and exposure heatmaps, adds expert and PII-category displays, and restructures appendix results from wide cross-task matrices into tables organized by dataset.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important gap through doctor-written reference summaries and adds useful data-construction and access information. However, it removes statistical-test reporting and introduces consequential inconsistencies: Section 6 reports 12% Llama location leakage while Table 4 shows 1.0%, and main-text Llama-3.3 labels conflict with appendix Llama-3.1 labels. The added evidence is valuable, but these reporting problems prevent a reliable judgment that its benefits outweigh the losses in evidential clarity.
